lead: M-ary FSK and QAM both send several bits per symbol, but they spend different resources. M-ary FSK picks one of M orthogonal tones: constant envelope and low power per bit, but a band that grows with M. QAM picks one point on a grid of amplitude and phase: many bits per hertz, but it needs a linear amplifier and a cleaner channel. Telemetry and some military and underwater links use M-ary FSK; Wi-Fi, cable modems and microwave backhaul use QAM.

sections.h3: M-ary FSK: one tone per symbol

blocks.text: M-ary FSK sends k = log<sub>2</sub> M bits by choosing one of M tones for a symbol time T<sub>s</sub> = kT<sub>b</sub>. The symbol rate is R<sub>s</sub> = R<sub>b</sub>/k.

The tones must be orthogonal over T<sub>s</sub>: the spacing is 1/(2T<sub>s</sub>) = R<sub>s</sub>/2 for coherent detection and 1/T<sub>s</sub> = R<sub>s</sub> for non-coherent detection. The receiver is a bank of M correlators (or M filters and envelope detectors); the largest output names the symbol, which maps back to k bits.
B is the occupied band in Hz. The bandwidth efficiency R<sub>b</sub>/B = 2k/M (coherent) falls as M grows: 1 b/s/Hz for M = 2 and 4, 0.75 for 8, 0.5 for 16.
the union bound for coherent orthogonal MFSK, with E<sub>s</sub> = kE<sub>b</sub> the symbol energy. Every wrong symbol is equally likely, so P<sub>b</sub> = P<sub>s</sub>·(M/2)/(M − 1).

At a fixed Eb/N0 the error rate of orthogonal MFSK falls as M grows, because Es = kEb grows while the distance between any two tones stays √(2Es). That makes MFSK power-efficient and bandwidth-hungry, the opposite of PSK and QAM.
I and Q are the in-phase and quadrature amplitudes in volts, chosen from a set of levels each symbol.

In square M-QAM, I and Q are independent √M-level amplitudes. For 16-QAM the levels are ±a and ±3a on each axis, a 4 × 4 grid; 4-QAM is QPSK. With Gray labels on each axis (00 → −3a, 01 → −a, 11 → +a, 10 → +3a), neighbours in the grid differ in one bit.

items: Group the bits in fours (for 16-QAM); the first two pick I and the last two pick Q.
Map each pair to its level with the Gray table above.
Multiply I by cos(2πf<sub>c</sub> t) and Q by sin(2πf<sub>c</sub> t) in two balanced modulators.
Subtract the Q product from the I product: s(t) = I cos − Q sin.

blocks.text: The coherent receiver has two correlators, one per carrier, and slices each output with thresholds at −2a, 0 and +2a. The average symbol energy of square M-QAM is E<sub>s</sub> = 2(M − 1)a²/3: 10a² for 16-QAM and 42a² for 64-QAM, in units where a point (I, Q) has energy I² + Q².
for square M-QAM at moderate to high E<sub>s</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>, with Gray labels P<sub>b</sub> ≈ P<sub>s</sub>/log<sub>2</sub> M.

With rectangular pulses the passband null-to-null bandwidth is 2R<sub>s</sub>, so the efficiency is k/2 b/s/Hz: 2 for 16-QAM, 3 for 64-QAM. Ideal Nyquist (sinc) pulses would need only R<sub>s</sub>, giving k b/s/Hz.

more errors, less band per bit

blocks.text: A saturating amplifier squeezes the outer QAM points inward and they land in the wrong decision regions; MFSK does not care. Choose QAM when spectrum is scarce and the signal-to-noise ratio is high, MFSK when power is scarce, the amplifier is nonlinear or non-coherent detection is wanted.

examples.question: A 16-QAM link carries 20 Mb/s with rectangular pulses and Gray labels at E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub> = 10 dB. Find the symbol rate, the null-to-null bandwidth and efficiency, the point that carries the bits 1011, and the symbol and bit error probabilities.
steps: Bits 10 → I = +3a; bits 11 → Q = +a. The point is (3a, a), on the right edge, one row above the axis.
Check: QPSK at the same 10 dB has P<sub>b</sub> = 3.87 × 10<sup>−6</sup>, so the doubled efficiency costs about 450 times the bit errors.
examples.answer: R<sub>s</sub> = 5 Msymbol/s, B = 10 MHz, 2 b/s/Hz; 1011 → (3a, a); P<sub>s</sub> ≈ 7.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup>, P<sub>b</sub> ≈ 1.75 × 10<sup>−3.</sup>

examples.question: An 8-FSK telemetry link sends 3 kb/s with coherent detection at E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub> = 8 dB. Find the symbol rate, the tone spacing, the bandwidth and efficiency, and bound the symbol and bit error probabilities.
steps: Coherent spacing 1/(2T<sub>s</sub>) = 500 Hz; B ≈ M·R<sub>s</sub>/2 = 8 × 500 = 4 kHz; efficiency 3/4 = 0.75 b/s/Hz.

Check: binary coherent FSK at 8 dB gives Q(√6.31) = 6.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup>; going to M = 8 lowered the error rate more than 200 times while the band grew only from about 3 kHz (1.5 kHz spacing at 3 kbaud) to 4 kHz.
examples.answer: R<sub>s</sub> = 1 ksymbol/s, spacing 500 Hz, B ≈ 4 kHz, 0.75 b/s/Hz, P<sub>s</sub> ≤ 4.75 × 10<sup>−5</sup>, P<sub>b</sub> ≤ 2.71 × 10<sup>−5.</sup>

traps: Bits per symbol are log<sub>2</sub> M: 16-QAM carries 4 bits, not 16.
Square M-QAM has √M levels per axis: 64-QAM has 8 levels on I and 8 on Q, not 64 on one axis.
The QAM formula uses E<sub>s</sub> = kE<sub>b</sub>. Putting E<sub>b</sub> in its place makes 16-QAM look 6 dB worse than it is.
MFSK bandwidth grows with M; it is the power-efficient scheme, not the bandwidth-efficient one.
Using R<sub>s</sub>/2 (the baseband Nyquist minimum) as a passband null-to-null bandwidth gives an efficiency of 2k (8 b/s/Hz for 16-QAM) instead of k/2 (2 b/s/Hz).

quiz.q: How many bits does a 64-QAM symbol carry, and how many levels per axis?
quiz.a: 6 bits; 8 levels on each of I and Q.

quiz.q: Why does the bandwidth of M-ary FSK grow with M?
quiz.a: Each of the M orthogonal tones needs its own slot at least R<sub>s</sub>/2 wide, so the band is about M·R<sub>s</sub>/2 while the bit rate grows only as log<sub>2</sub> M.

quiz.q: Why does orthogonal MFSK make fewer errors as M grows at fixed E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>?
quiz.a: E<sub>s</sub> = kE<sub>b</sub> grows with k, and every pair of tones stays √(2E<sub>s</sub>) apart, so the distances grow faster than the number of competitors.

quiz.q: 64-QAM sends 30 Mb/s with rectangular pulses. Find R<sub>s</sub> and the null-to-null bandwidth.
List the 16-QAM levels and thresholds on one axis, and find E<sub>s</sub> for a = 1.
Compare 16-QAM and coherent 16-FSK at 20 Mb/s in bandwidth.
quiz.a: Both have R<sub>s</sub> = 5 Msymbol/s. 16-QAM: 2R<sub>s</sub> = 10 MHz. 16-FSK: 16 × 2.5 = 40 MHz (80 MHz non-coherent). QAM needs a quarter of the band but more power and a linear amplifier.

quiz.q: Why must a QAM transmitter use a linear amplifier?
quiz.a: Information sits in amplitude too; compression moves the outer points inward across decision thresholds and also spreads the spectrum.

beyond: Not for the exam. Wi-Fi 6 and 7 reach 1024-QAM and 4096-QAM, and 4G and 5G switch between QPSK and 256-QAM as the channel changes (adaptive modulation). Digital predistortion lets QAM transmitters run amplifiers closer to saturation. MFSK survives in deep-space, HF and underwater acoustic modems. Search next: adaptive modulation and coding, PAPR, digital predistortion.
